shortItems.brief: At the checkout, a customer checks the labels on two similar cards in her wallet, chooses the one marked for personal spending, and pays with it.

storyPattern.interaction: Pause to compare two similar cards and state which one she wants to use
storyPattern.outcome: Pay with the card marked for personal spending

shortItems.brief: Two housemates see an electricity bill on the table. One puts money in an envelope labeled for the bill, and the other agrees they will not use that money for other expenses.

storyPattern.goal: Keep money intended for a household bill separate from other spending
storyPattern.interaction: Label an envelope and explain what the reserved money is for
storyPattern.outcome: Both housemates leave the bill money untouched

shortItems.brief: A tenant shows her landlord that the bedroom window rattles in the wind. He tightens the loose latch, and she closes the window to check that it is quieter.

storyPattern.goal: Stop a bedroom window from rattling
storyPattern.interaction: Describe and demonstrate the noise before a small adjustment
storyPattern.outcome: Test the window and find it quieter

shortItems.brief: A resident calls the municipal service desk to report a streetlight that is not working and gives the street names when the worker asks which corner it is on. The worker records the location.

storyPattern.goal: Report a streetlight that is not working
storyPattern.interaction: The resident reports the problem, and the worker asks which corner; she gives the street names
storyPattern.outcome: The worker records the streetlight's location

shortItems.brief: Dana asks Ron which coworker will call the customer back. Ron takes responsibility for the call and writes the customer's name on a note.

storyPattern.goal: Make sure a customer receives a promised call back
storyPattern.interaction: Check who is responsible and agree on one person to make the call

shortItems.brief: At the produce counter, a shopper asks for three apples instead of a full bag. The seller weighs them, she says the amount is right, and she puts the apples in her basket.

storyPattern.goal: Buy only a few pieces of weighed produce
storyPattern.interaction: State a small quantity and respond to the amount weighed
storyPattern.outcome: Accept the portion and put it in the basket

shortItems.brief: A shopper likes a jacket, tests whether her phone fits in its inside pocket, and buys it when it does.

storyPattern.goal: Check that a clothing item meets a practical need before buying
storyPattern.interaction: Test the pocket with her phone rather than relying on appearance
storyPattern.outcome: Choose the jacket after confirming the phone fits

shortItems.brief: A woman hears the delivery worker by the gate but cannot open the building entrance from her apartment. She asks him to call her, then comes down to meet him at the gate.

shortItems.brief: While updating her online account, the user sees that her chosen password is too short. She enters a longer password, the form accepts it, and she signs in.

shortItems.brief: A woman orders a salad and asks for a little dressing on the side. The server brings it in a small cup.

stories.brief: A 1998 documentary about experimental Israeli schools presents different approaches to learning: one school held history lessons at archaeological sites, another included students with and without intellectual disabilities, and a democratic school let students vote on its budget.

sources.title: Let the Sky be the Limit: Experimental Educational Institutions
Our History
Dewey and Israel’s Educational Philosophy and Practice

storyBeats: In 1998, the Israel Film Service made a 27-minute documentary about experimental schools in Israel for the Ministry of Education, Culture, and Sports.
The film’s archive description estimated that about 80 experimental schools were using new teaching methods in Israel by the late 1990s.
At the religious state school in Hoshaya, history lessons took place at archaeological sites rather than only in classrooms.
At Manshiya Zabda School, students without intellectual disabilities studied alongside students with intellectual disabilities.
At the democratic school in Hadera, students could vote on the school budget.
The documentary included perspectives from students, parents, teachers, and school principals.
The Hadera democratic school was founded in 1987 by Yaacov Hecht, parents, and educators, working with the municipality and the Ministry of Education.
Hadera’s first school year combined required lessons for half the day with elective lessons for the other half, following disagreement about how much freedom students should have.
After discussion in the school parliament, required hours were reduced; by the school’s third anniversary, the parliament voted to end all required class hours.
A scholarly account describes another Israeli experiment, Carmel Beach School at Ma’agan Michael, which opened in 1973 with many elective courses and mixed-age learning groups.

stories.brief: Israeli textile designer Hannah Barkai, born in Poland as Anna Brodacz, founded the Anbi weaving workshop in Tel Aviv in 1935, where she designed and made cloth and household textiles, taught women weaving, employed weavers, and later advised the Maskit company.

sources.title: Hannah Barkai Archive
Textile as Material and Visual Biography
Weaving History

storyBeats: Hannah Barkai was born Anna Brodacz in Poland in 1904 and later moved to Israel.
In 1935, she founded Anbi, a weaving workshop on Has Street in Tel Aviv, where she worked as both a textile designer and a weaver.
Anbi made woven textiles for clothing and household objects.
Barkai taught women weaving and employed weavers in the workshop.
She advised the Maskit company when it was established in 1954.
Anbi continued operating commercially until the early 1980s.
Barkai had a doctorate in chemistry from the Sorbonne in Paris before taking up weaving as a profession in Israel.
A study of Israeli textile design notes that Barkai’s early work used a modernist style, while traditional folk-embroidery images appeared in her designs after Israel’s establishment.
Anbi’s labels used an image of a weaving shuttle as a sign of the workshop’s textile work.
Barkai and her husband, architect Shmuel (Sam) Barkai, kept her papers and work materials at their Tel Aviv home; a representative selection was organized and digitized in 2021.

stories.brief: A 1967 Israeli Film Service documentary surveyed modern Israeli theatre through scenes from productions by Habima, Cameri, Haifa Theatre, and other companies, including plays and musicals staged that year.

sources.title: Theatre In Israel
The Musicals Rumpelstiltskin and King Solomon and Shalmai The Shoemaker at the Cameri Theater
Selected Filmography

storyBeats: The 26-minute documentary Theatre In Israel was made in 1967 by the Israel Film Service and directed by David Perlov.
Produced on behalf of the Israeli Center of the International Theater Institute, the English-speaking film introduced modern Israeli theatre to an international audience.
The film opens with scenes from The Dybbuk at Habima, featuring actors Hanna Rovina and Shimon Finkel.
It includes Cameri Theatre scenes from the musicals Utz Li Gutz Li, also known as Rumpelstiltskin, and King Solomon and Shalmai The Shoemaker.
The Cameri musical Rumpelstiltskin was directed by Yossi Yzraely and featured Shoshik Shani, Nira Rabinovich, Natan Cogan, and Esther Greenberg.
King Solomon and Shalmai The Shoemaker was directed by Shmuel Bonim and featured Illi Gorlitzky and Yona Atari.
The film also shows The American Princess by Nissim Aloni at the Seasons Theater, with Yossi Banai and Avner Chiskiyahu.
Its examples include Moshe Shamir’s He Walked Through the Fields at the Haifa Theater.
Other excerpts include Ibsen’s Hedda Gabler, starring Hannah Maron, and Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf?, starring Miriam Zohar and Misha Asherov.
The documentary was made in English and also had French-language material; the archive lists English and Hebrew subtitles.

stories.brief: On November 25, a report said Israel’s Health Ministry had formally recognized Ruth Children’s Hospital at Rambam in Haifa as a separate hospital specializing in children’s medicine; Professor Yael Shachor-Meyouhas was appointed director.

sources.title: Ruth Children’s Hospital at Rambam recognized as an independent hospital

teaser.text: לפי דיווח מ־25 בנובמבר, משרד הבריאות הכיר בבית החולים רות ברמב״ם כבית חולים עצמאי לילדים, ופרופ׳ יעל שחור-מיוחס מונתה למנהלת שלו.

translations.ru: Согласно сообщению от 25 ноября, Министерство здравоохранения признало детскую больницу «Рут» в медицинском центре «Рамбам» самостоятельной больницей, а профессора Яэль Шахор-Меюхас назначили ее директором.
translations.en: According to a report on November 25, the Health Ministry recognized Ruth Hospital at Rambam as an independent children's hospital, and Professor Yael Shachor-Meyouhas was appointed its director.

stories.brief: A 1998 documentary about experimental Israeli schools presents different approaches to learning: one school held history lessons at archaeological sites, another included students with and without intellectual disabilities, and a democratic school let students vote on its budget.

sources.title: Let the Sky be the Limit: Experimental Educational Institutions
Our History
Dewey and Israel’s Educational Philosophy and Practice

storyBeats: In 1998, the Israel Film Service made a 27-minute documentary about experimental schools in Israel for the Ministry of Education, Culture, and Sports.
The film’s archive description estimated that about 80 experimental schools were using new teaching methods in Israel by the late 1990s.
At the religious state school in Hoshaya, history lessons took place at archaeological sites rather than only in classrooms.
At Manshiya Zabda School, students without intellectual disabilities studied alongside students with intellectual disabilities.
At the democratic school in Hadera, students could vote on the school budget.
The documentary included perspectives from students, parents, teachers, and school principals.
The Hadera democratic school was founded in 1987 by Yaacov Hecht, parents, and educators, working with the municipality and the Ministry of Education.
Hadera’s first school year combined required lessons for half the day with elective lessons for the other half, following disagreement about how much freedom students should have.
After discussion in the school parliament, required hours were reduced; by the school’s third anniversary, the parliament voted to end all required class hours.
A scholarly account describes another Israeli experiment, Carmel Beach School at Ma’agan Michael, which opened in 1973 with many elective courses and mixed-age learning groups.

stories.brief: Israeli textile designer Hannah Barkai, born in Poland as Anna Brodacz, founded the Anbi weaving workshop in Tel Aviv in 1935, where she designed and made cloth and household textiles, taught women weaving, employed weavers, and later advised the Maskit company.

sources.title: Hannah Barkai Archive
Textile as Material and Visual Biography
Weaving History

storyBeats: Hannah Barkai was born Anna Brodacz in Poland in 1904 and later moved to Israel.
In 1935, she founded Anbi, a weaving workshop on Has Street in Tel Aviv, where she worked as both a textile designer and a weaver.
Anbi made woven textiles for clothing and household objects.
Barkai taught women weaving and employed weavers in the workshop.
She advised the Maskit company when it was established in 1954.
Anbi continued operating commercially until the early 1980s.
Barkai had a doctorate in chemistry from the Sorbonne in Paris before taking up weaving as a profession in Israel.
A study of Israeli textile design notes that Barkai’s early work used a modernist style, while traditional folk-embroidery images appeared in her designs after Israel’s establishment.
Anbi’s labels used an image of a weaving shuttle as a sign of the workshop’s textile work.
Barkai and her husband, architect Shmuel (Sam) Barkai, kept her papers and work materials at their Tel Aviv home; a representative selection was organized and digitized in 2021.

teaser.text: חנה ברקאי הקימה בתל אביב סדנת אריגה, שבה יצרו בדים ולימדו נשים לארוג.

translations.ru: Ханна Баркай открыла в Тель-Авиве мастерскую ткачества, где создавали ткани и учили женщин ткать.
translations.en: Hannah Barkai founded a weaving workshop in Tel Aviv, where people made fabrics and taught women to weave.

stories.brief: A 1967 Israeli Film Service documentary surveyed modern Israeli theatre through scenes from productions by Habima, Cameri, Haifa Theatre, and other companies, including plays and musicals staged that year.

sources.title: Theatre In Israel
The Musicals Rumpelstiltskin and King Solomon and Shalmai The Shoemaker at the Cameri Theater
Selected Filmography

storyBeats: The 26-minute documentary Theatre In Israel was made in 1967 by the Israel Film Service and directed by David Perlov.
Produced on behalf of the Israeli Center of the International Theater Institute, the English-speaking film introduced modern Israeli theatre to an international audience.
The film opens with scenes from The Dybbuk at Habima, featuring actors Hanna Rovina and Shimon Finkel.
It includes Cameri Theatre scenes from the musicals Utz Li Gutz Li, also known as Rumpelstiltskin, and King Solomon and Shalmai The Shoemaker.
The Cameri musical Rumpelstiltskin was directed by Yossi Yzraely and featured Shoshik Shani, Nira Rabinovich, Natan Cogan, and Esther Greenberg.
King Solomon and Shalmai The Shoemaker was directed by Shmuel Bonim and featured Illi Gorlitzky and Yona Atari.
The film also shows The American Princess by Nissim Aloni at the Seasons Theater, with Yossi Banai and Avner Chiskiyahu.
Its examples include Moshe Shamir’s He Walked Through the Fields at the Haifa Theater.
Other excerpts include Ibsen’s Hedda Gabler, starring Hannah Maron, and Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf?, starring Miriam Zohar and Misha Asherov.
The documentary was made in English and also had French-language material; the archive lists English and Hebrew subtitles.
